Even now, through all its joints, the gangrene of a bloody war creeps. It is no different in the whole world. Think on these things, Lipsius, and through this sharing of miseries, lighten your own. And just as a servant used to be placed behind those celebrating a triumph, who would cry out repeatedly in the midst of the joy of the triumph, **"You are a man"**: so let this monitor always stand by you, saying, **"These things are human."** For just as labor shared with many becomes lighter, so also does grief.

### CHAPTER XXVI.

->*The Conclusion of the whole discourse, and a brief admonition to repeat and reflect upon it.*<-

I have set forth all my forces and my discourse, Lipsius. You have what I judged should be said to you on behalf of <term>Constantia</term> <gloss>Constancy</gloss> against <term>Dolor</term> <gloss>Grief or Pain</gloss>. May these things be not only pleasing to you, but healing; and may they not merely delight, but rather help! They will help, however, if you let them sink not only into your ears, but into your soul; and if you do not allow what you have heard to lie idle and wither away, like seeds scattered on the surface of the soil. <summary>Langius concludes his discourse by urging Lipsius to view his personal suffering as part of the universal human condition and to deeply internalize these Stoic lessons through constant reflection.</summary>
